text: Every automation in this chapter eventually gets touched by someone who didn't build it, a new admin, a consultant, or you yourself eighteen months from now with no memory of why a rule exists. Working today isn't the same as maintainable tomorrow.

A validation rule named Rule_1 tells the next person nothing. One named for its object, purpose, and condition tells them what it does without opening it. The same goes for approval processes, email alerts, and flow. Pick a convention before the org has fifty of these, because renaming later touches every single reference.

The formula itself already documents what a rule checks. It doesn't document why, and why is almost always what breaks when someone fixes it later without context. The Description field should capture the business reason it exists, any non-obvious edge case, and what would actually break if it were removed.

Validation rules, approval processes, and workflow rules can all be deactivated without being deleted, turned off but still present, still documented, still restorable in seconds. Deleting is permanent. The practical rule: deactivate first, watch for a full business cycle if you can manage it, and only delete once you're confident nothing depended on it silently.

Automation piling up on one object isn't automatically wrong, but it's a cost that compounds. Three signs it's time to consolidate: you can't predict the order several automations run in without checking a reference every time, two or more of them read or write the same field, or new admins keep asking why there are three rules doing almost the same thing. And consolidation itself needs sandbox testing, don't treat cleanup as lower-risk than a new feature.

That closes Chapter 2, and the choice between declarative and code, the order everything runs in, and what keeps it maintainable once it's live. Chapter 3 puts all of it to work on two real, end-to-end case studies.
